prompt: In what way are nitriles analogous to carboxylic acids?

choices.text: Both have a carbon with three bonds to an electronegative atom, plus a π bond
Both have an acidic O–H hydrogen that bases can remove
choices.why: A nitrile, RC≡N, has no O–H group.

choices.text: Both have an sp3-hybridized carbon in the functional group
choices.why: The carboxyl carbon is sp2, and the nitrile carbon is part of a triple bond. Neither is sp3.

choices.text: Both are nucleophiles, so both react readily with electrophiles
choices.why: Both are electrophiles, and both undergo nucleophilic addition reactions.

explanation: Nitriles and carboxylic acids both have a carbon atom with three bonds to an electronegative atom, and both contain a π bond. So both are electrophiles, and both undergo nucleophilic addition reactions.

prompt: What happens when a cyanogenic glycoside is hydrolyzed with aqueous acid?

choices.text: Its acetal is cleaved to give a cyanohydrin, which releases hydrogen cyanide
Its nitrile is hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid, which releases ammonia
choices.why: The section says the acetal is cleaved, generating a cyanohydrin (HO–C–CN) that releases HCN.

choices.text: Its nitrile is reduced to a primary amine
choices.why: Reduction needs a hydride reagent such as LiAlH4. Aqueous acid cleaves the acetal.

choices.text: Its nitrile carbon bonds to a sugar oxygen to form a new acetal
choices.why: Hydrolysis breaks the acetal apart rather than forming one.

explanation: Cyanogenic glycosides contain a sugar acetal carbon, one oxygen of which is bonded to a nitrile-bearing carbon (sugar–O–C–CN). Aqueous acid cleaves the acetal, giving a cyanohydrin (HO–C–CN) that releases HCN. This probably protects the plant by poisoning animals that eat it.

prompt: What product forms when 2-ethylhexanamide is heated with thionyl chloride, SOCl2, in benzene at 80 °C?

choices.why: SOCl2 dehydrates the primary amide; it doesn't hydrolyze it.
An amine would come from a reduction, such as LiAlH4 reduction of a nitrile.
Dehydration adds no carbon. The amide carbon becomes the nitrile carbon.

explanation: Primary amides, RCONH2, are dehydrated to nitriles by thionyl chloride. 2-Ethylhexanamide gives 2-ethylhexanenitrile in 94% yield, along with SO2 and HCl.

prompt: When a primary amide, RCONH2, is dehydrated with SOCl2, the by-products are SO2 and HCl. How many equivalents of HCl form per equivalent of nitrile?
explanation: RCONH2 + SOCl2 → RC≡N + SO2 + 2 HCl. The two N–H hydrogens and the two chlorines of SOCl2 end up as two HCl, and the amide oxygen leaves in the SO2.

prompt: Why is nitrile synthesis by amide dehydration more general than S_N2 displacement by CN− on an alkyl halide?

choices.text: It is not limited by steric hindrance
It adds one carbon to the chain
choices.why: Amide dehydration adds no carbon; the amide carbon becomes the nitrile carbon. It's the S_N2 route that adds a carbon from CN−.

choices.text: It needs no reagent other than heat
choices.why: A dehydrating agent such as SOCl2 or POCl3 is used.

choices.text: It works on alkyl halides of every kind
choices.why: Amide dehydration starts from a primary amide, RCONH2, not an alkyl halide.

explanation: Both methods are useful, but the S_N2 route is limited to primary or secondary alkyl halides. The synthesis from amides is more general because it is not limited by steric hindrance.

prompt: Which method would better prepare 2,2-dimethylpropanenitrile, (CH3)3CC≡N?

choices.why: Cyanide displacement works on primary and secondary alkyl halides. (CH3)3CBr is tertiary and too hindered.
That would put a CH2 group between the tert-butyl group and the nitrile, giving (CH3)3CCH2C≡N.
Aqueous acid hydrolyzes nitriles to carboxylic acids, not the reverse.

explanation: The nitrile carbon is attached to a tertiary carbon, so the S_N2 route would need the tertiary halide (CH3)3CBr, which is too hindered. Dehydrating the primary amide (CH3)3CCONH2 with SOCl2 is not limited by steric hindrance.

prompt: What forms when a nucleophile adds to the carbon of a nitrile?

choices.why: That forms when a nucleophile adds to a carbonyl group. Addition to C≡N gives an imine anion, which still has a C=N bond.
The imine anion keeps a C=N double bond, so its carbon is sp2.
The nucleophile adds to the electrophilic carbon and the electrons move onto nitrogen, giving an anion.

explanation: Like a carbonyl group, a nitrile group is strongly polarized and has an electrophilic carbon. Nucleophiles add to give sp2-hybridized imine anions, analogous to the sp3-hybridized alkoxide ions formed by addition to a carbonyl group.

prompt: Nitrile hydrolysis in aqueous acid or base ends with a carboxylic acid. What compound forms first, on the way?

choices.why: Amines come from reducing nitriles with LiAlH4, not from hydrolysis.
Ketones form when a Grignard reagent adds to a nitrile and the imine anion is then hydrolyzed.
Hydrolysis adds water to the C≡N group, giving an amide and then an acid. No alcohol forms.

explanation: Nitrile hydrolysis yields first an amide and then a carboxylic acid plus ammonia or an amine. It occurs in either basic or acidic aqueous solution.

prompt: In base-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis, OH− adds to the C≡N bond and the imine anion is protonated to a hydroxy imine. What happens to the hydroxy imine next?

choices.text: It loses NH2− to give a carboxylate ion
choices.why: NH2− leaves later, from the tetrahedral alkoxide ion formed when OH− adds to the amide.

choices.text: It is reduced to a primary amine
choices.why: No reducing agent is present. Reduction to an amine needs LiAlH4.
The step resembles enol-to-ketone tautomerization, but here the hydroxy imine becomes an amide.

explanation: Protonation of the imine anion gives a hydroxy imine, which tautomerizes to an amide in a step similar to the tautomerization of an enol to a ketone. Further hydrolysis then gives a carboxylate ion (Figure 20.7.2).

prompt: In basic hydrolysis of the amide intermediate, OH− adds to the amide carbonyl to give a tetrahedral alkoxide ion. What leaving group is expelled next?

choices.why: Losing OH− would just reverse the addition. Expelling NH2− is what gives the carboxylate.
The group leaves as the amide ion, NH2−, which then takes a proton to become ammonia.
The C≡N bond has already been converted into the amide, so no cyanide is released.

explanation: Hydroxide adds to the amide carbonyl group, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide ion. Expulsion of amide ion, NH2−, as the leaving group gives the carboxylate ion (with ammonia) and drives the reaction toward products. Acidification in a separate step gives the carboxylic acid.

prompt: Propanenitrile, CH3CH2C≡N, is heated with aqueous NaOH, and the solution is then acidified. What organic product is isolated?

choices.why: The amide is only an intermediate. With heating in aqueous base it is hydrolyzed on to the carboxylate, which acidification turns into the acid.
Amines come from LiAlH4 reduction, not from hydrolysis.
Hydrolysis adds no carbon. The nitrile carbon becomes the carboxyl carbon.

explanation: Basic hydrolysis converts the nitrile, by way of the amide, into the carboxylate ion plus ammonia. Acidification in a separate step gives propanoic acid.

prompt: Benzonitrile, C6H5C≡N, is treated with LiAlH4, and water is added in a second step. What is the product?

choices.why: Benzoic acid would come from hydrolysis in aqueous acid or base. LiAlH4 reduces the nitrile.
With LiAlH4, hydride adds twice to the C≡N bond, giving an amine after protonation.
The nitrile carbon is kept. It becomes the CH2 of the amine, C6H5CH2NH2.

explanation: Reduction of a nitrile with LiAlH4 gives a primary amine: the nitrile carbon becomes a CH2 bonded to NH2. Hydride adds twice to the C≡N bond to give a dianion, and water then protonates it. Benzonitrile gives benzylamine.

prompt: In the LiAlH4 reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine, how many hydride ions add to the nitrile carbon?
explanation: Hydride adds to the C≡N bond to give an imine anion. That anion still contains a C=N bond, so a second hydride adds, giving a dianion. Water then protonates the dianion to the amine.

prompt: In the LiAlH4 reduction of a nitrile, what makes the second hydride addition possible when it would otherwise be difficult?

choices.text: Lewis acid–base complexation of the anion intermediates to an aluminum species
Protonation of the imine anion by water before the second addition
choices.why: Water is added only in a later step, to protonate the dianion.

choices.text: Hydrogen-bonding between the imine anion and a second nitrile molecule
choices.why: The section credits complexation of the anions to aluminum, not hydrogen-bonding.

choices.text: Tautomerization of the imine anion to an amide
choices.why: Amide formation happens in hydrolysis, not in LiAlH4 reduction.

explanation: Both the monoanion and dianion intermediates are undoubtedly stabilized by Lewis acid–base complexation to an aluminum species, which helps the second hydride addition that would otherwise be difficult.

prompt: Benzonitrile, C6H5C≡N, reacts with ethylmagnesium bromide, CH3CH2MgBr, in ether, and the mixture is then hydrolyzed with aqueous acid. What is the product?

choices.why: Only one nucleophilic addition occurs to the nitrile. Hydrolysis of the imine anion then gives a ketone.
The ethyl group from the Grignard reagent stays on the former nitrile carbon, so the product is a ketone, not an acid.
Water hydrolyzes the imine anion to a ketone and ammonia; nothing reduces it to an amine.

explanation: A Grignard reagent adds once to a nitrile to give an imine anion, and hydrolysis gives a ketone. The C≡N carbon becomes the carbonyl carbon, bonded to the phenyl group from the nitrile and the ethyl group from the Grignard reagent: C6H5COCH2CH3 (propiophenone).

prompt: How many nucleophilic additions to the nitrile carbon occur when a Grignard reagent reacts with a nitrile?
explanation: The reaction resembles LiAlH4 reduction, except that only one nucleophilic addition occurs rather than two, and the nucleophile is a carbanion (R:^−) rather than a hydride ion. Hydrolysis of the imine anion then gives a ketone.

prompt: Which nitrile and Grignard reagent, followed by H3O+, would give 2-methyl-3-pentanone, (CH3)2CHCOCH2CH3?

choices.why: Two ethyl groups on the carbonyl carbon give 3-pentanone, CH3CH2COCH2CH3.
Two isopropyl groups give (CH3)2CHCOCH(CH3)2, not the target.
This gives CH3COCH2CH(CH3)2, whose carbonyl carbon carries methyl and isobutyl groups.

explanation: The C≡N carbon becomes the carbonyl carbon, with one group from the nitrile and the other from the Grignard reagent. 2-Methyl-3-pentanone has ethyl and isopropyl groups on its carbonyl carbon, so propanenitrile and isopropylmagnesium bromide work. Isobutyronitrile, (CH3)2CHC≡N, with ethylmagnesium bromide is the other route in Worked Example 20.7.1.

prompt: Which nitrile and Grignard reagent, followed by H3O+, would give the ketone p-ClC6H4COCH3?

choices.why: That gives acetone, CH3COCH3. The chlorophenyl group has to come from one of the reactants.
An ethyl Grignard reagent gives p-ClC6H4COCH2CH3, with an ethyl group rather than a methyl on the carbonyl carbon.
That gives C6H5COCH3, which lacks the chlorine.

explanation: The carbonyl carbon carries a p-chlorophenyl group and a methyl group. Taking the chlorophenyl group from the nitrile (p-chlorobenzonitrile) and the methyl group from the Grignard reagent (CH3MgBr), then adding H3O+, gives the ketone (Exercise 20.7.1b).

prompt: Which sequence converts benzyl bromide, C6H5CH2Br, into 1-phenyl-2-butanone, C6H5CH2COCH2CH3?

choices.why: A methyl Grignard reagent gives C6H5CH2COCH3, one carbon short. The ketone needs an ethyl group.
LiAlH4 reduces the nitrile to a primary amine, C6H5CH2CH2NH2.
Heating with aqueous acid first hydrolyzes the nitrile to phenylacetic acid. The Grignard reagent must add to the nitrile to make the ketone.

explanation: S_N2 displacement by CN− gives C6H5CH2C≡N. Ethylmagnesium bromide adds to the nitrile carbon, and hydrolysis of the imine anion gives the ketone C6H5CH2COCH2CH3 (Exercise 20.7.2).

prompt: Butanenitrile, CH3CH2CH2C≡N, reacts with CH3MgBr, and the product is hydrolyzed with H3O+. How many carbon atoms does the ketone contain?
explanation: All four carbons of the nitrile are kept, with the C≡N carbon becoming the carbonyl carbon, and the Grignard reagent adds one methyl carbon: CH3CH2CH2COCH3, 2-pentanone, with 5 carbons.
